name: ATMEGA328P-AU
title: ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/P 8-bit AVR microcontrollers, 4 to 32 Kbytes Flash, 1.8 V to 5.5 V, up to 20 MHz
summary: A family of 8-bit AVR RISC microcontrollers that run most of their 131 instructions in one clock, giving close to 1 MIPS per MHz up to 20 MHz from a 1.8 V to 5.5 V supply. The members differ in memory: 4, 8, 16 or 32 Kbytes of self-programmable Flash, 256 bytes to 1 Kbyte of EEPROM and 512 bytes to 2 Kbytes of SRAM, with a separate boot section and read-while-write on all but the 48A/48PA. Each carries two 8-bit and one 16-bit timer, six PWM outputs, a USART, SPI, a two-wire (I2C-compatible) interface, a 10-bit ADC with 6 or 8 inputs, an analog comparator, a watchdog and six sleep modes, with 23 I/O lines. ATMEGA328P-AU is the 32 Kbyte picoPower part in the 32-lead TQFP.
key_figures: 8-bit AVR, 32 x 8 working registers, up to 20 MIPS at 20 MHz, 2-cycle hardware multiplier
32 Kbytes Flash, 1 Kbyte EEPROM, 2 Kbytes SRAM
0.1 µA / 0.75 µA (32 kHz RTC running) at 1.8 V, 25 °C
10-bit, 8 channels in TQFP and VQFN, 6 in SPDIP, with temperature measurement
23 programmable I/O lines, pin-change interrupt on every port pin

circuits.title: Crystal or ceramic resonator on XTAL1/XTAL2
circuits.description: A quartz crystal or ceramic resonator sits between XTAL1 and XTAL2, the input and output of the on-chip inverting amplifier, with a capacitor from each pin to ground. C1 and C2 are kept equal. For crystals the starting range is 12 pF to 22 pF from 0.9 MHz up (low power oscillator) or 0.4 MHz to 20 MHz (full swing oscillator); a ceramic resonator takes the values its maker gives. The same hook-up drives the 32.768 kHz low-frequency oscillator and, on TOSC1/TOSC2, the Timer/Counter2 oscillator.

circuits.title: External clock drive
circuits.description: An external clock signal drives XTAL1 with CKSEL set to 0000, from 0 to 20 MHz. XTAL2 is not used by the clock and stays free as the port pin PB7. Cycle-to-cycle frequency changes must stay under 2%.

circuits.title: ADC power connections
circuits.description: The analog supply pin AVCC is fed from the digital VCC through a 10 µH series inductor and is decoupled to ground by a 100 nF capacitor at the pin, forming an LC filter that keeps digital supply noise off the ADC. The filter, the ADC pins and the GND pin next to AREF sit over an analog ground plane.

operation.text: ATmega48A/PA, 88A/PA, 168A/PA and 328/P hold 4, 8, 16 and 32 Kbytes of Flash (32 KB on the 328P), 256, 512, 512 and 1024 bytes of EEPROM (1 KB on the 328P) and 512, 1024, 1024 and 2048 bytes of SRAM (2 KB on the 328P). The core is the AVR, an 8-bit RISC design: 131 instructions, most of them one clock long, 32 working registers, fully static, and a two-cycle multiplier, reaching 20 MIPS at 20 MHz.

23 programmable I/O lines. Peripherals: two 8-bit timer/counters and one 16-bit, a real-time counter with its own oscillator, six PWM outputs, a 10-bit ADC (eight inputs in TQFP and VQFN, six in SPDIP) that can also measure temperature, a USART, master/slave SPI, a byte-wide two-wire interface compatible with I2C, an analog comparator, a watchdog with its own oscillator and pin-change wake-up. Supply 1.8 V to 5.5 V, -40 °C to 85 °C.

Ports B and D are 8 bits wide and Port C 7 bits (PC6 is the reset pin unless RSTDISBL is programmed). Every port pin has a pull-up that can be turned on per bit, and output drivers that sink and source equally hard. An input with its pull-up on sources current when held low from outside. All port pins go to high impedance as soon as a reset starts, without needing a running clock.

AVCC feeds the ADC, PC3:0 and ADC7:6, while PC6:4 take their supply from VCC. AVCC is tied to VCC even when the ADC is idle, through a low-pass filter when it is used. AREF is the converter's reference pin. ADC6 and ADC7 exist only in the TQFP and VQFN packages, as analog-only 10-bit inputs on the analog supply.

Idle halts the CPU while SRAM, timers, USART, two-wire interface, SPI and interrupts keep working. Power-down keeps register contents and stops the oscillator, so only an interrupt or a hardware reset brings the part back. Power-save keeps the asynchronous timer running as a time base. ADC Noise Reduction stops the CPU and every I/O module but the asynchronous timer and the ADC to quieten conversions. Standby leaves the crystal or resonator oscillator running for a very fast start-up at low current.

The Flash can be rewritten in the system over SPI, with an ordinary non-volatile memory programmer, or from a boot program on the chip, which may load the application over any interface. Code in the Boot Flash section keeps running while the Application section is written (read-while-write).

Memory sizes, boot loader support and vector size are the only things that set the eight devices apart (one word per vector on 48/88, two on 168/328). Every device but ATmega48A/48PA has a separate boot loader section from which alone SPM runs, giving read-while-write self-programming. ATmega48A/48PA have neither read-while-write nor a boot section, and SPM runs from anywhere in the Flash.
Reliability qualification projects a retention failure rate far below 1 PPM: for 20 years at 85 °C, and for 100 years at 25 °C.

Harvard architecture: program and data have their own memories and buses. A single-level pipeline fetches the next instruction while the current one executes, so an instruction can complete every clock. The 32 x 8-bit register file is read and written in one cycle: two operands out, ALU operation, result back, all in one clock. R26 to R31 pair up as the 16-bit pointers X, Y and Z for indirect data addressing, and Z can also point into Flash for look-up tables.

operation.topic: Program flow, stack and I/O space
operation.text: Jumps and calls reach the whole address space; instructions are 16 or 32 bits, mostly 16. The Flash splits into a boot program section and an application section, each with its own lock bits; the SPM instruction that writes the application section must sit in the boot section. Return addresses go on a stack in SRAM, so stack depth is limited only by free SRAM, and the reset routine must set up SP before any call or interrupt. Interrupt priority follows vector address, lowest first. The 64 I/O addresses are reached directly or as data addresses 0x20 to 0x5F; the extended I/O space at 0x60 to 0xFF answers only to ST/STS/STD and LD/LDS/LDD.

The ALU does arithmetic, logic and bit operations between registers or between a register and a constant in a single clock, and also single-register operations; a multiplier handles signed and unsigned numbers and fractional format. SREG updates after every ALU operation, often making a separate compare unnecessary. SREG is neither saved on entry to an interrupt nor restored on return; software does that. Its bits: I (global interrupt enable, cleared by hardware when an interrupt is taken and set again by RETI; SEI and CLI also set and clear it), T (bit store for BLD and BST), H (half carry, for BCD), S (N exclusive-or V), V (two's complement overflow), N (negative), Z (zero), C (carry).

The register file supports one 8-bit operand with an 8-bit result, two 8-bit operands with an 8-bit or a 16-bit result, and one 16-bit operand with a 16-bit result. Each register also occupies one of the first 32 data addresses, so X, Y and Z can index any register. The X, Y and Z pointers support fixed displacement, post-increment and pre-decrement.
The stack grows from high to low addresses: PUSH decrements SP. SP starts at the last SRAM address (RAMEND) and must point above 0x0100, the start of SRAM. It is two 8-bit I/O registers, SPH and SPL.
The CPU clock clkCPU comes straight from the selected clock source with no internal division. Fetch and execute overlap, giving up to 1 MIPS per MHz.

Every interrupt has its own vector and its own enable bit, which works only together with the I bit in SREG. Programming the boot lock bits BLB02 or BLB12 can turn interrupts off depending on where the program counter is. The vectors sit at the bottom of program memory, RESET first and INT0 next in priority. Setting IVSEL in MCUCR relocates the vectors to where the Boot Flash section begins; the BOOTRST fuse relocates the reset vector likewise. Taking an interrupt clears I, so nesting needs software to set I again; RETI sets it. Flag-type interrupts set a flag that hardware clears on entry to the handler (or software clears by writing one); a flag raised while the interrupt or I is off waits and is served by priority once enabled. Level-type interrupts last only as long as their condition, without needing a flag. After RETI one instruction of the main program always runs before a pending interrupt is served. CLI takes effect at once, even against a simultaneous interrupt; after SEI the next instruction runs before any pending interrupt.

At least four clocks pass before the vector runs, during which the program counter is pushed; the usual jump at the vector adds three clocks. A multi-cycle instruction in progress is completed first. Waking from sleep adds four clocks on top of the sleep mode's start-up time. RETI takes four clocks: the two-byte program counter is popped, SP rises by two and I is set.

4, 8, 16 or 32 Kbytes, organised as 2, 4, 8 or 16K x 16 since every instruction is 16 or 32 bits wide; the program counter is 11, 12, 13 or 14 bits. Endurance is at least 10,000 write/erase cycles. Except on 48A/48PA the space divides into a Boot Loader section and an Application section for software security. Constant tables may sit anywhere in program memory and are read with LPM.

The lowest data addresses cover, in order, 32 working registers, 64 I/O addresses, 160 extended I/O addresses and then 512, 1024, 1024 or 2048 bytes of SRAM, all reachable by every addressing mode: direct (whole data space), indirect, indirect with displacement (63 locations past the base in Y or Z), and indirect with pre-decrement or post-increment on X, Y and Z.
An SRAM access takes two clkCPU cycles. Reading the EEPROM stops the CPU for four clocks before the next instruction; writing it stops the CPU for two.

256, 512, 512 or 1024 bytes in their own data space, byte-wise readable and writable, with at least 100,000 write/erase cycles. Writes follow a set procedure to stop accidental ones, and a self-timing flag tells software when the next byte may be written.

At too low a VCC an EEPROM write may fail, and the CPU itself may run instructions wrongly. Holding the part in reset while the supply is too low avoids both: the internal brown-out detector does this, or an external low-VCC reset circuit where the BOD levels do not fit. A write in progress when reset arrives completes if the voltage is enough.

All I/O and peripheral registers are in the I/O space, reachable with LD/LDS/LDD and ST/STS/STD. Registers at 0x00 to 0x1F are bit-addressable with SBI and CBI and testable with SBIS and SBIC; SBI and CBI change only the named bit, so they are safe on registers holding flags that clear when written with one. IN and OUT use I/O addresses 0x00 to 0x3F; as data addresses these sit 0x20 higher. Reserved bits are written as zero and reserved addresses are never written. Three general purpose I/O registers hold any data, those in 0x00 to 0x1F being bit-accessible.

clkCPU runs the core: register file, status register and the stack's data memory. clkI/O runs most I/O modules (timers, SPI, USART) and the external interrupt logic. clkFLASH runs the Flash interface, normally alongside clkCPU. clkASY lets the asynchronous timer/counter run from an external clock or a 32 kHz crystal, so it can keep real time in sleep. clkADC is a separate domain so that CPU and I/O clocks can be stopped to cut noise during conversions. Sleep modes stop the clocks of unused modules.

Parts ship running from the internal RC oscillator at 8.0 MHz with CKDIV8 programmed, giving a 1.0 MHz system clock, with the longest start-up time and the time-out on (CKSEL = 0010, SUT = 10, CKDIV8 = 0).

After every other reset source releases, an internal reset holds for a time-out tTOUT counted on the watchdog oscillator, its length set by the SUT and CKSEL fuses; the watchdog oscillator frequency varies with voltage. The time-out does not watch VCC, so it must be longer than the VCC rise; where that is not possible a brown-out detector is used, which then allows the time-out to be turned off. A ripple counter then holds reset for a set number of oscillator cycles, from 6 for an external clock to 32K for a low-frequency crystal. From reset both delays apply; on waking from Power-save or Power-down only the oscillator start-up applies.

XTAL1 and XTAL2 are the input and output of an inverting amplifier for a quartz crystal or ceramic resonator. This oscillator swings XTAL2 less, using the least power, but cannot drive other clock inputs and may suffer more in noisy surroundings. C1 and C2 are equal; their best value depends on the crystal, stray capacitance and noise. CKSEL3..1 picks one of three frequency ranges and CKSEL0 with SUT1..0 the start-up time.
Drives XTAL2 rail to rail, so it can clock other parts and copes better with noise, at higher current than the low power oscillator. It works only with VCC from 2.7 V to 5.5 V.

Built for a 32.768 kHz watch crystal and for very low current, so crystal load capacitance and ESR both matter. Each TOSC pin has internal capacitance, and a crystal with CL above 6 pF needs external capacitors as well. It is selected with CKSEL 0100 or 0101, and SUT sets the start-up delay.

Gives about 8.0 MHz with no external parts; the frequency moves with voltage and temperature. At reset hardware loads the factory calibration byte into OSCCAL; writing OSCCAL from software can calibrate more closely. When this oscillator clocks the chip, the watchdog oscillator still times the watchdog and the reset time-out.
A low power 128 kHz source, nominal at 3 V and 25 °C, selected with CKSEL 0011.

A clock fed to XTAL1 with CKSEL 0000 runs the part. A frequency step of more than 2% between one cycle and the next can upset operation, so larger changes are made with the part held in reset, or by the system clock prescaler.

Programming the CKOUT fuse puts the system clock on CLKO (PB0), overriding the pin's normal use and continuing during reset. Any clock source may be used; with the prescaler active, the divided clock comes out.

The low-frequency crystal oscillator doubles as the Timer/Counter2 oscillator on TOSC1/TOSC2, which share the XTAL1 and XTAL2 pins. The system clock must be four times the oscillator frequency; with that and the shared pins, the timer oscillator is usable only when the calibrated internal RC oscillator is the system clock. Setting EXTCLK in ASSR lets an external clock drive TOSC1 instead of a crystal.

CLKPR divides the system clock (clkI/O, clkADC, clkCPU, clkFLASH) for any clock source, to save power when less speed is needed. Changing the setting causes no glitch and no intermediate frequency above either the old or the new one. The prescaler's ripple counter runs at the undivided clock and cannot be read, so the switch time is not exactly predictable. A change is made by writing CLKPCE to one with the other CLKPR bits zero, then within four cycles writing the new CLKPS with CLKPCE zero, with interrupts off.

Setting SE in SMCR and executing SLEEP enters the mode chosen by SM2..0. An enabled interrupt wakes the part, which halts for four cycles plus the start-up time, runs the handler and continues after the SLEEP instruction; register file and SRAM keep their contents. A reset during sleep wakes the part to the reset vector. With the BOD enabled it keeps watching VCC through sleep.

On ATmega48PA/88PA/168PA/328P only, software can switch the brown-out detector off for some sleep modes through BODS (bit 6 of MCUCR, written by a timed sequence), bringing sleep current down to the fused-off level. The BOD stops just after sleep is entered and comes back on by itself at wake-up; the wake-up then takes about 60 µs so the BOD is working before code resumes. BODS is zero by default.

SM2..0 = 000. The CPU and Flash clocks stop; SPI, USART, comparator, ADC, two-wire interface, timers, watchdog and interrupts keep running, so internal events such as timer overflow or USART transmit complete can wake the part as well as external ones. Switching the comparator off with ACD in ACSR saves current when its wake-up is not needed. An enabled ADC starts a conversion on entry.

SM2..0 = 001. clkI/O, clkCPU and clkFLASH stop; the ADC, external interrupts, two-wire address watch, Timer/Counter2 (asynchronous mode only) and watchdog keep running. An enabled ADC starts a conversion on entry. Wake sources: ADC conversion complete, external reset, watchdog reset or interrupt, brown-out reset, two-wire address match, Timer/Counter2 interrupt, SPM/EEPROM ready, INT0 or INT1 at a low level, or any pin change.

SM2..0 = 010. The external oscillator stops; external interrupts, two-wire address watch and watchdog still work. Only external reset, watchdog reset or interrupt, brown-out reset, two-wire address match, INT0 or INT1 at a low level, or any pin change wake it; only asynchronous modules run. A level interrupt used to wake must stay present until start-up ends, or the part wakes without taking the interrupt. The wake-up delay is set by the same CKSEL fuses as the reset time-out.

SM2..0 = 011. As Power-down, but an enabled Timer/Counter2 keeps running and its overflow or compare interrupt can wake the part (with the enable bits in TIMSK2 and I in SREG set). Without Timer/Counter2 running, Power-down is the better choice. The timer oscillator stops in sleep unless Timer2 uses the asynchronous clock, and the synchronous clock source stops unless Timer2 uses it; even when running, that clock serves only Timer/Counter2.
SM2..0 = 110 with a crystal or resonator clock selected. As Power-down with the oscillator left running; wake-up takes six clock cycles.
SM2..0 = 111 with a crystal or resonator clock selected. As Power-save with the oscillator left running; wake-up takes six clock cycles.

PRR stops the clock of single peripherals. A stopped peripheral keeps its state and its registers cannot be read or written; resources it holds stay held, so it is normally disabled first. Clearing its PRR bit brings it back in the same state. This helps in Active and Idle modes; the other sleep modes stop those clocks anyway.

Use sleep as much as possible, in the deepest mode the application allows, with unneeded functions off. An enabled ADC stays on in every sleep mode, so turn it off first; the next conversion after re-enabling is an extended one. Turn the comparator off in Idle when unused and always in ADC Noise Reduction; in other modes it switches off by itself unless it uses the internal reference. A BOD enabled by fuses runs in every sleep mode and adds markedly to deep-sleep current, as does an enabled watchdog.

operation.topic: Internal reference, port pins and debug in sleep
operation.text: The internal reference runs whenever the BOD, comparator or ADC needs it and stops when they are off; after turning it back on, allow its start-up time before using it. In sleep, pins should not drive resistive loads. Where clkI/O and clkADC both stop, input buffers are disabled except where needed for wake-up; an enabled input left floating or near VCC/2 draws excess current, so digital inputs on analog pins should stay off at all times (DIDR0, DIDR1). With debugWIRE enabled by the DWEN fuse, the main clock keeps running in sleep and adds to current.

Reset returns all I/O registers to their initial values and starts the program at the reset vector, which holds a JMP on 168A/168PA/328/328P and an RJMP on 48A/48PA and 88A/88PA. Vector locations of unused interrupts may hold ordinary code, as may the vector table when the reset vector and vectors are in different sections (88 and up). I/O ports reset to their initial state the moment a reset source asserts, with no clock needed. Once every source has released, a delay counter set by SUT and CKSEL stretches the internal reset so the supply can settle.

Four: power-on reset (VCC below VPOT), external reset (RESET held low longer than the minimum pulse width), watchdog system reset (watchdog period expires in system reset mode), and brown-out reset (VCC below VBOT with the BOD enabled). MCUSR records which one occurred (PORF, EXTRF, BORF, WDRF).

An on-chip detector asserts reset while VCC is below its level, both at start-up and when the supply fails. Crossing the level on the way up starts the delay counter that holds the part in reset; falling below it asserts reset again at once, with no delay. RESET may be tied to VCC or held low externally to extend start-up.

A low on RESET longer than the minimum pulse width resets the part, clock or not; shorter pulses may not. When the pin rises through VRST, the delay counter starts and the part runs after tTOUT. The RSTDISBL fuse turns external reset off.

The on-chip BOD compares VCC with a level chosen by the BODLEVEL fuses, with hysteresis. Below VBOT− brown-out reset asserts at once; above VBOT+ the delay counter releases the part after tTOUT. A dip is caught only if it lasts longer than tBOD.
A watchdog time-out produces a reset pulse one CK cycle long, whose falling edge starts the tTOUT delay.

A bandgap reference serves the brown-out detector and can feed the comparator or the ADC. It runs only when the BOD is enabled by its fuses, when ACBG in ACSR connects it to the comparator, or when the ADC is enabled; otherwise it is off. Without the BOD, allow its start-up time after setting ACBG or enabling the ADC; avoiding all three before Power-down keeps it off.

Counts cycles of its own 128 kHz on-chip oscillator, with time-outs from 16 ms to 8 s. WDR restarts the count. Three modes: interrupt (wake from sleep, or a general timer such as a limit on how long an operation may run), system reset (recovery from runaway code), and interrupt then reset (for saving state before the reset). The WDTON fuse forces system reset mode with WDE locked to 1 and WDIE to 0. Clearing WDE or changing the time-out needs a timed sequence: write WDCE and WDE to one together, then within four clocks write WDE and WDP as wanted with WDCE zero, in one write.

A watchdog switched on by accident (a stray pointer, a brown-out) resets the part and stays on, which can loop through time-out resets if code does not expect it. Clearing WDRF and WDE early in initialisation avoids this, watchdog used or not.
Reset the watchdog before changing WDP: moving to a shorter period may otherwise time out at once.

The four device pairs share one vector list. Each vector is two words on 168A/168PA and 328/328P and one word on 48A/48PA and 88A/88PA. 48A/48PA have no boot section; on the others BOOTRST moves the reset vector and IVSEL in MCUCR moves the start of the interrupt vectors.
Where no interrupt is enabled the vector area may hold program code, as it may when reset vector and interrupt vectors sit in different sections (one in application Flash, the other in boot Flash).

INT0 and INT1 trigger on a falling edge, a rising edge or a low level, set in EICRA; a low-level interrupt repeats as long as the pin stays low. PCINT23..0 trigger on any toggle: PCI2 covers PCINT23:16, PCI1 PCINT14:8 and PCI0 PCINT7:0, with PCMSK2, PCMSK1 and PCMSK0 choosing the pins. All of them fire even with the pin set as an output, which gives a way to raise a software interrupt. Pin-change, low-level and INT0/INT1 edge interrupts are detected asynchronously and so can wake the part from sleep modes other than Idle, where clkI/O is stopped. A level used to wake from Power-down must last until start-up is over, or the part wakes without taking the interrupt.

Port pins have true read-modify-write: SBI and CBI change one pin's direction, value or pull-up without touching the others. Drivers sink and source equally and are strong enough for LED displays directly. Pull-ups are selectable per pin, with resistance that does not change with supply voltage. Every pin has protection diodes to VCC and ground. Each port has three registers: PORTx (data), DDRx (direction), both read/write, and PINx (input, read-only); writing a one to a PINx bit toggles the matching PORTx bit. PUD in MCUCR turns every pull-up off. Enabling an alternate function on some pins leaves the rest of the port usable as general I/O.

DDxn = 1 makes the pin an output, driven high or low by PORTxn. DDxn = 0 makes it an input, with PORTxn = 1 turning the pull-up on; PORTxn = 0 or making the pin an output turns it off. Pins go to high impedance when reset asserts, even without a clock. Writing one to PINxn toggles PORTxn whatever DDxn holds.

Going between tri-state (00) and output high (11) passes through pull-up on (01) or output low (10). The pull-up state normally does no harm; if it does, PUD can disable all pull-ups. Moving from pulled-up input to output low, or back, needs tri-state or output high as the step between.

PINxn reads the pin whatever DDxn holds, through a latch and flip-flop that act as a synchronizer against metastability. An outside change reaches PINxn after between 1/2 and 1 1/2 system clock periods. Reading back a value software has just written needs a NOP between the write and the read; the delay is then one clock period.

In Power-down, Power-save and Standby the sleep controller clamps each digital input to ground ahead of the Schmitt trigger so floating or mid-level inputs draw no current. Pins enabled as external interrupts are exempt, as are pins claimed by some alternate functions. A high level on an asynchronous interrupt pin set for rising edge, falling edge or any change, with the interrupt not enabled, sets its flag on leaving such a sleep mode, because the clamp looks like a change.

Unused pins should sit at a defined level to save current in reset, Active and Idle, where digital inputs are on. The internal pull-up is the simplest way, though it is off during reset; for low current in reset an external resistor to either rail does the job. Tying unused pins straight to VCC or GND risks heavy current if the pin is ever set as an output.

Alternate functions take over a pin through override signals generated in the module concerned: pull-up, direction, output value, toggle and digital input enable each have an enable and a value, plus the digital input DI and the analog connection AIO. Not every pin has every override.

Used as XTAL2 or XTAL1 (every clock source except the calibrated RC oscillator uses XTAL1), PB7/PB6 are lost as I/O and DDB, PORTB and PINB for them read 0. As TOSC2/TOSC1 they serve only with the calibrated RC oscillator as system clock and AS2 in ASSR set (with EXCLK clear for a crystal on TOSC2): the pins leave the port and become the amplifier output and input. SPI: as slave, SCK, MOSI and SS are inputs whatever DDB holds; as master, MISO is an input whatever DDB holds; a pin forced to input by the SPI keeps its pull-up under PORTB control. As slave the SPI is active while SS is low. OC2A (PB3), OC1B (PB2) and OC1A (PB1) need DDB set to output and also carry PWM. PB0 is ICP1, and with CKOUT programmed outputs the divided system clock, also during reset, regardless of PORTB0 and DDB0. Every Port B pin is also a pin-change interrupt source.

With RSTDISBL programmed PC6 is ordinary I/O and reset comes only from power-on and brown-out; unprogrammed it is the reset pin, lost as I/O, with DDC6, PORTC6 and PINC6 reading 0. With TWEN in TWCR set, PC5 and PC4 leave the port and become SCL and SDA, driven open drain with slew-rate limiting and with a spike filter that suppresses input spikes shorter than 50 ns. ADC inputs 5 and 4 run from the digital supply; ADC inputs 3 to 0 from the analog supply. Every Port C pin is also a pin-change interrupt source.

AIN1 (PD7) and AIN0 (PD6) are used as inputs with the pull-up off so the port does not disturb the comparator. OC0A (PD6), OC0B (PD5) and OC2B (PD3, Timer/Counter2 compare match B) need DDD set to output and also carry PWM. T1 (PD5) and T0 (PD4) are counter inputs; XCK (PD4) is the USART clock. INT1 (PD3) and INT0 (PD2) are the external interrupts. With the USART transmitter on, TXD (PD1) is an output whatever DDD1 holds; with the receiver on, RXD (PD0) is an input whatever DDD0 holds, its pull-up still under PORTD0. Every Port D pin is also a pin-change interrupt source.

An 8-bit timer/counter with two independent output compare units (A and B) whose compare registers are double buffered. It offers clear-on-compare (auto reload), glitch-free phase correct PWM, a variable PWM period and a frequency generator, with three interrupt sources: TOV0, OCF0A and OCF0B. The module runs only while PRTIM0 in the power reduction register is 0.

TCNT0, OCR0A and OCR0B are 8-bit registers. Its interrupt flags live in TIFR0 and each is masked in TIMSK0. The count clock clkT0 comes from the shared prescaler or from an external signal on pin T0, chosen by CS02:0 in TCCR0B; with no source selected (CS02:0 = 0) the timer stands still, though the CPU can still read and write TCNT0. A CPU write to TCNT0 wins over any clear or count in the same cycle. Each timer clock the counter is cleared, incremented or decremented according to the mode, which WGM01:0 in TCCR0A and WGM02 in TCCR0B select; TOV0 is set at a point that also depends on the mode.

TCNT0 is compared with OCR0A and OCR0B all the time; an equal value sets OCF0A or OCF0B on the following timer clock, which can raise an interrupt. The flag clears when its vector runs, or when software writes a one to it. In the PWM modes OCR0x is double buffered and the compare register takes the new value only at TOP or BOTTOM, which keeps the PWM pulses symmetrical and free of odd lengths; in Normal and CTC modes the CPU writes OCR0x directly. In the non-PWM modes writing a one to FOC0x acts on the OC0x pin as a real match would (set, clear or toggle per COM0x1:0) without setting the flag or clearing the timer. Any CPU write to TCNT0 suppresses a compare match in the next timer clock, even with the timer stopped, so OCR0x can be loaded with the TCNT0 value without an interrupt. Writing TCNT0 equal to OCR0x therefore loses that match, and writing BOTTOM while counting down should be avoided. Set up OC0x before switching the pin to output (FOC0x in Normal mode is the simplest way); OC0x keeps its state across mode changes. COM0x1:0 is not buffered and acts at once.

When either COM0x1:0 bit is non-zero the waveform generator's OC0x drives the pin in place of the port, but the pin is an output only if its DDR bit is set. This override does not depend on the waveform mode. A system reset clears the internal OC0x register. COM0x1:0 = 0 means no action on the next match; a new COM0x1:0 setting takes effect at the first match after it is written, or immediately through FOC0x in the non-PWM modes. Some COM0x1:0 values are reserved in some modes.

WGM02:0 = 0. The counter only counts up and rolls over from 0xFF to 0x00, setting TOV0 in the timer clock where TCNT0 becomes zero; TOV0 then works as a ninth bit that is set but never cleared by hardware, and with the overflow interrupt clearing it software can extend the resolution. TCNT0 may be written at any time. The compare units can time interrupts, but generating waveforms this way is not recommended because of the CPU load.

WGM02:0 = 2. The counter clears to zero when TCNT0 equals OCR0A, so OCR0A sets TOP and the resolution; OCF0A can interrupt at each TOP and its handler may change TOP. This mode has no double buffering of OCR0A: written below the current TCNT0 with a fast timer clock, the match is missed and the counter runs to 0xFF and wraps before matching. With COM0A1:0 = 1 OC0A toggles on each match, giving at most fclk_I/O/2 with OCR0A = 0; the pin shows it only when set as output. TOV0 is set as the counter passes from MAX to 0x00.

WGM02:0 = 3 (TOP = 0xFF) or 7 (TOP = OCR0A). Single slope: the counter runs BOTTOM to TOP and clears on the next timer clock. Non-inverting (COM0x1:0 = 2) clears OC0x at the match and sets it at BOTTOM; inverting (3) does the opposite. Its frequency can be twice that of phase correct PWM, which suits power regulation, rectification and DAC uses with small external parts. TOV0 is set at each TOP. COM0A1:0 = 1 with WGM02 = 1 toggles OC0A on matches, giving a 50 % square wave of at most fclk_I/O/2 with OCR0A = 0 and with the compare register double buffered; OC0B has no toggle option. OCR0A = BOTTOM gives a narrow spike every MAX+1 timer clocks; OCR0A = MAX holds the output steady high or low according to COM0A1:0.

WGM02:0 = 1 (TOP = 0xFF) or 5 (TOP = OCR0A). Dual slope: the counter runs BOTTOM to TOP, stays at TOP for one timer clock and runs back down. Non-inverting output clears OC0x at the match while counting up and sets it at the match while counting down; inverting does the opposite. The frequency is lower than single slope, but the symmetry is preferred for motor control. TOV0 is set at each BOTTOM. Non-inverting, OCR0A = BOTTOM keeps the output low and OCR0A = MAX keeps it high; inverting gives the reverse. COM0A1:0 = 1 with WGM02 = 1 toggles OC0A; OC0B has no toggle option. To stay symmetrical about BOTTOM, OCnx can change state with no match at the start of a period in two cases: when OCR0A moves away from MAX, and when the timer starts above the compare value and so misses the up-counting match.

The timer is synchronous; clkT0 acts as a clock enable on clkI/O. TOV0 is set in the cycle where TCNT0 moves from MAX to BOTTOM. OCF0x is set one timer clock after TCNT0 equals OCR0x (OCF0B in every mode; OCF0A in every mode but CTC and the PWM mode where OCR0A is TOP). In CTC mode and in fast PWM with OCR0A as TOP, TCNT0 clears to BOTTOM in the timer clock after it reaches TOP, as OCF0A is set.

A true 16-bit timer/counter (16-bit PWM) with two independent double-buffered output compare units, one input capture unit with a noise canceler, clear-on-compare, glitch-free phase correct PWM, a variable PWM period, a frequency generator and an external event counter. Four interrupt sources: TOV1, OCF1A, OCF1B and ICF1. The module runs only while PRTIM1 in PRR is 0. Its count clock comes from the prescaler or pin T1 (CS12:0 in TCCR1B); the capture input is pin ICP1 or the analog comparator.

TCNT1, OCR1A, OCR1B and ICR1 are 16-bit; TCCR1A and TCCR1B are 8-bit with no access restriction. Flags are in TIFR1, masks in TIMSK1. TOP can be one of the fixed values 0x00FF, 0x01FF or 0x03FF, or the value in OCR1A or ICR1, according to the mode. With OCR1A as TOP in a PWM mode, OC1A cannot produce PWM, but TOP is then double buffered and can change while running; ICR1 as TOP leaves OCR1A free for PWM on OC1A.

The CPU reaches the 16-bit registers one byte at a time over the 8-bit bus. Each 16-bit timer has one TEMP register for the high byte, shared by all its 16-bit registers, and the low-byte access is what triggers the transfer. To write, give the high byte first: writing the low byte copies TEMP and the low byte into the register in one clock. To read, take the low byte first: reading it copies the high byte into TEMP in the same clock. Reading OCR1A or OCR1B does not use TEMP. If an interrupt routine also touches any 16-bit register of the timer, the main program has to disable interrupts around its own two-byte access, or the shared TEMP is corrupted. When several registers are written with the same high byte, the high byte needs writing only once (still under the same atomic-access rule). A C compiler handles the byte order itself.

TCNT1 is split into TCNT1H and TCNT1L; the CPU sees TCNT1H only through TEMP, which is loaded from TCNT1H when TCNT1L is read and copied into TCNT1H when TCNT1L is written, so the whole count moves in one clock. Some writes to TCNT1 while counting give unpredictable results (named in the mode descriptions). CS12:0 = 0 stops the counter; TCNT1 stays accessible and a CPU write beats a clear or count. The count sequence follows WGM13:0 in TCCR1A and TCCR1B, and TOV1 is set according to the mode.

An edge on ICP1, or on the analog comparator output ACO, that matches the edge setting copies the 16-bit TCNT1 into ICR1 and sets ICF1 in the same system clock; with ICIE1 = 1 it raises an interrupt. ICF1 clears when the vector runs or by writing a one to it. Read ICR1L before ICR1H. ICR1 can be written only in a waveform mode that uses it as TOP, after WGM13:0 is set, high byte first. ACIC in ACSR selects the comparator as trigger; changing the source can itself cause a capture, so clear ICF1 afterwards. ICP1 and ACO are sampled and edge-detected like the T1 pin. The noise canceler and edge detector input stays enabled except in modes where ICR1 sets TOP. Software can trigger a capture by driving the ICP1 port bit.

Set by ICNC1 in TCCR1B, the noise canceler is a digital filter that needs four equal successive samples before its output changes. It adds four system clocks of delay between an input change and the ICR1 update, and runs on the system clock, so the prescaler does not affect it.

ICR1 is overwritten by the next event if software has not read it, so read it as early as possible in the interrupt; the worst-case response depends on the longest other interrupt handler. Capturing while TOP is being changed is not recommended. To measure duty cycle, switch the trigger edge after every capture, as soon as ICR1 has been read, and then clear ICF1 by writing a one; to measure frequency alone, an interrupt handler need not clear ICF1.

TCNT1 is compared with OCR1x continuously; a match sets OCF1x on the following timer clock and, with OCIE1x = 1, raises an interrupt. Unit A can also set TOP, which fixes both the resolution and the waveform period. OCR1x is double buffered in all twelve PWM modes, synchronised to TOP or BOTTOM, and accessed directly in Normal and CTC modes. Only CPU writes change OCR1x, so it is read without TEMP (low byte first is still good practice), but it is written through TEMP, high byte first, because all 16 bits are compared continuously. FOC1x forces a match result in non-PWM modes without setting the flag or clearing the timer. A write to TCNT1 blocks any match in the next timer clock even when stopped. Do not write TCNT1 equal to OCR1x (the match is lost), equal to TOP in a PWM mode with variable TOP (the TOP match is ignored and the counter runs on to 0xFFFF), or equal to BOTTOM while counting down. Set OC1x before making the pin an output; OC1x keeps its state across mode changes; COM1x1:0 changes act at once.

A non-zero COM1x1:0 hands the pin to OC1x, with the DDR bit still deciding whether it is driven. The override is mostly independent of the waveform mode, with exceptions in the compare output mode tables. Reset clears the OC1x register. A new COM1x1:0 acts at the next match (immediately via FOC1x in non-PWM modes). COM1x1:0 has no effect on input capture.

WGM13:0 = 0. Counts up only and rolls over from 0xFFFF to 0x0000, setting TOV1 as TCNT1 becomes zero; TOV1 behaves like a 17th bit that hardware never clears. Input capture is simple in this mode, but the time between events must not exceed the counter range, or the overflow interrupt or the prescaler is needed to extend it. Waveform output from the compare units in this mode costs too much CPU time to be recommended.

WGM13:0 = 4 (TOP = OCR1A) or 12 (TOP = ICR1). The counter clears when TCNT1 equals TOP; OCF1A or ICF1, whichever register defines TOP, can interrupt at TOP. There is no double buffering, so a new TOP written below the running TCNT1 misses the match and the counter wraps through 0xFFFF; fast PWM with OCR1A as TOP (WGM13:0 = 15) avoids this because OCR1A is buffered there. With COM1A1:0 = 1, OC1A toggles on each match (pin visible with DDR_OC1A = 1), up to fclk_I/O/2 at OCR1A = 0. TOV1 is set as the count passes from MAX to 0x0000.

WGM13:0 = 5, 6 or 7 (fixed TOP 0x00FF, 0x01FF, 0x03FF: 8, 9 or 10 bits), 14 (TOP = ICR1) or 15 (TOP = OCR1A). Resolution runs from 2 bits (TOP = 0x0003) to 16 bits (TOP = MAX). Single slope, so up to twice the frequency of the dual-slope modes. Non-inverting COM1x1:0 = 2, inverting 3. TOV1 is set at each TOP, and OCF1A or ICF1 in the same clock when that register is TOP; a handler may then update TOP and compare values. A new TOP must not be below any compare register, or those matches never occur; with a fixed TOP, unused OCR1x bits are masked to zero on write. ICR1 is not buffered, so lowering it while running can miss TOP and send the counter round through 0xFFFF; OCR1A is buffered and its compare register loads at the next TOP, as TCNT1 clears and TOV1 sets. ICR1 as TOP suits a fixed frequency and frees OC1A; when the frequency changes on the fly OCR1A as TOP is the better choice. OCR1x = BOTTOM gives a narrow spike every TOP+1 timer clocks; OCR1x = TOP holds the output constant. COM1A1:0 = 1 toggles OC1A at 50 % only with WGM13:0 = 15, up to fclk_I/O/2 at OCR1A = 0.

WGM13:0 = 1, 2 or 3 (fixed 8, 9 or 10 bits), 10 (TOP = ICR1) or 11 (TOP = OCR1A); 2-bit to 16-bit resolution. Dual slope with one timer clock at TOP. TOV1 is set at BOTTOM; OCF1A or ICF1 is set at TOP, when the buffered compare values load. Because OCR1x updates at TOP, the falling slope follows the old TOP and the rising slope the new one, so changing TOP while running can make a period asymmetrical; phase and frequency correct mode is recommended then, and with a fixed TOP the two modes behave practically alike. TOP must stay at or above every compare value; fixed TOP masks unused OCR1x bits. Non-inverting COM1x1:0 = 2, inverting 3. Non-inverting, OCR1x = BOTTOM holds the output low and OCR1x = TOP holds it high. With WGM13:0 = 11 and COM1A1:0 = 1, OC1A toggles at 50 %.

operation.topic: Timer/Counter1 phase and frequency correct PWM mode
operation.text: WGM13:0 = 8 (TOP = ICR1) or 9 (TOP = OCR1A); 2-bit to 16-bit resolution. Dual slope like phase correct mode, but the compare registers load from their buffers at BOTTOM, with TOV1 set in the same clock, so both slopes of every period are always equal and the output is symmetrical in all periods. OCF1A or ICF1 is set when TCNT1 reaches TOP. TOP must stay at or above every compare value. ICR1 as TOP suits a fixed frequency; OCR1A as TOP suits a changing one. Non-inverting, OCR1x = BOTTOM holds the output low and OCR1x = TOP sets it high; inverting gives the reverse. With WGM13:0 = 9 and COM1A1:0 = 1, OC1A toggles at 50 %.

clkT1 acts as a clock enable on clkI/O. OCF1x is set one timer clock after TCNT1 equals OCR1x. In CTC and fast PWM the count goes TOP to BOTTOM; in the dual-slope modes it turns at TOP (TOP-1, TOP, TOP-1). TOV1 in fast PWM, and ICF1 when ICR1 is TOP, are set at TOP, where buffered OCR1x values take effect. In phase and frequency correct mode OCR1x updates at BOTTOM, and the same timing then holds with BOTTOM in place of TOP; the same substitution applies to TOV1 in the modes that set it at BOTTOM.

Both timers share one prescaler but choose their settings separately. CSn2:0 = 1 clocks the timer straight from the system clock, the fastest option (fCLK_I/O); the four prescaler taps give fCLK_I/O/8, /64, /256 and /1024. The prescaler runs freely whatever the timers select, so after a timer is started on a tap, the first count arrives 1 to N+1 system clocks later (N = 8, 64, 256 or 1024). Resetting the prescaler (PSRSYNC) can align a timer with program execution, but it changes the prescaler phase for both timers at once.

operation.topic: External clock on T0 and T1
operation.text: Pin T1 or T0 can clock its timer: the pin is sampled every system clock by a synchroniser (a latch transparent while clkI/O is high, then registers on the rising edge) and an edge detector that issues one count per rising edge (CSn2:0 = 7) or falling edge (CSn2:0 = 6). An edge reaches the counter 2.5 to 3.5 system clocks after it arrives. Switch the clock input on or off only when the pin has been steady for at least one system clock, or a false count may result. Each half period of the external clock must exceed one system clock; with 50 % duty the frequency must be under fclk_I/O/2, and because oscillator and capacitor tolerances move the system clock, staying below fclk_I/O/2.5 is recommended. An external clock cannot be prescaled.

An 8-bit timer/counter with two compare outputs (OC2A, OC2B), clear-on-compare, glitch-free phase correct PWM, a frequency generator, a 10-bit prescaler and three interrupt sources (TOV2, OCF2A, OCF2B). It can be clocked from a 32 kHz watch crystal on its own oscillator, apart from the I/O clock. The module runs only while PRTIM2 in PRR is 0. TCNT2, OCR2A and OCR2B are 8-bit; flags are in TIFR2 and masks in TIMSK2. Its clock is clkI/O through the prescaler by default, or the oscillator on TOSC1/TOSC2 when AS2 in ASSR is one; ASSR controls the asynchronous operation.

The counter, compare units and compare match output work as in Timer/Counter0: CS22:0 = 0 stops the clock; WGM21:0 in TCCR2A and WGM22 in TCCR2B set the sequence; a match sets OCF2x one timer clock later; OCR2x is double buffered only in PWM modes; FOC2x forces a match result in non-PWM modes; a TCNT2 write blocks the next match; non-zero COM2x1:0 hands the pin to OC2x, which drives it only when its DDR bit is set; COM2x1:0 changes act at once.

Normal (WGM22:0 = 0): counts up, rolls over at 0xFF, TOV2 as a ninth bit. CTC (WGM22:0 = 2): clears at OCR2A, with no double buffering, so a TOP written below TCNT2 is missed and the counter wraps through 0xFF; COM2A1:0 = 1 toggles OC2A, up to fclk_I/O/2 at OCR2A = 0. Fast PWM (WGM22:0 = 3, TOP = 0xFF; or 7, TOP = OCR2A): single slope, TOV2 at TOP, non-inverting COM2x1:0 = 2, inverting 3; COM2A1:0 = 1 with WGM22 = 1 toggles OC2A at 50 %; OCR2A = BOTTOM gives a narrow spike every MAX+1 timer clocks and OCR2A = MAX a constant level. Phase correct PWM (WGM22:0 = 1 or 5): dual slope, TOV2 at BOTTOM; non-inverting, OCR2A = BOTTOM keeps the output low and MAX keeps it high; the output may switch at the start of a period with no match, when OCR2A leaves MAX or when the timer starts above OCR2A. The prescale factor N is 1, 8, 32, 64, 128, 256 or 1024.

Synchronous operation is the same as Timer/Counter0, clkT2 acting as a clock enable; in asynchronous mode the Timer/Counter oscillator clock takes the place of clkI/O. OCF2A is set one timer clock after the match in every mode but CTC; in CTC TCNT2 clears after TOP as OCF2A sets.

Switching Timer/Counter2 between synchronous and asynchronous clocking can corrupt TCNT2, OCR2x and TCCR2x. A safe order: disable its interrupts (OCIE2x, TOIE2); set AS2; write TCNT2, OCR2x and TCCR2x; when going asynchronous, wait for TCN2UB, OCR2xUB and TCR2xUB to clear; clear the Timer/Counter2 interrupt flags; re-enable interrupts as needed. The CPU clock has to exceed the oscillator frequency by a factor above four. A write to TCNT2, OCR2x or TCCR2x goes to a temporary register (one per register) and lands after two rising TOSC1 edges; do not write the same register again before then; the busy flags in ASSR show when the transfer is done. Before entering Power-save or ADC Noise Reduction with Timer/Counter2 as the wake source, wait for the written register to update; the compare function is off while OCR2x or TCNT2 is being written, so sleeping too soon can mean no compare interrupt and no wake-up. Re-entering those modes within one TOSC1 cycle of a wake-up causes repeated interrupts; writing TCCR2x, TCNT2 or OCR2x and waiting for its busy flag to clear guarantees a full TOSC1 cycle has passed.

With asynchronous operation selected the 32.768 kHz oscillator keeps running in every mode except Power-down and Standby. After power-up or a wake from Power-down or Standby it may need up to one second to settle, so wait at least one second before using the timer, and treat all Timer/Counter2 registers as lost after such a wake, whether a crystal or a clock on TOSC1 is used. On a wake from Power-save or ADC Noise Reduction the counter has always moved on by one or more counts by the time the CPU can read it; the MCU halts four cycles, runs the interrupt routine and continues after the SLEEP instruction. TCNT2 is read through a register synchronised on each rising TOSC1 edge, so just after a wake it can still show the value from before sleep; to read it reliably, write OCR2x or TCCR2x, wait for that busy flag to clear, then read TCNT2. Interrupt flag synchronisation takes three processor cycles plus one timer cycle. The compare output pin changes on the timer clock, not in step with the CPU clock.

The Timer/Counter2 clock clkT2S is clkI/O by default; with AS2 in ASSR set it comes from TOSC1, Timer/Counter2 can serve as a real-time counter, and TOSC1 and TOSC2 leave Port B so a crystal between them can clock the timer independently. The oscillator is optimised for a 32.768 kHz crystal. The prescaler offers clkT2S/8, /32, /64, /128, /256 and /1024, plus clkT2S itself and stop. Setting PSRASY in GTCCR resets the prescaler so its phase is known.

A synchronous serial port for fast transfers to peripherals or other AVR devices: full duplex over three wires, master or slave, LSB or MSB first, seven bit rates (the system clock divided by 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 or 128, with SPI2X giving the doubled rates), an end-of-transmission interrupt flag, write collision protection, wake-up from Idle, and double-speed (CK/2) master mode. The USART can also act as an SPI master. The module runs only while PRSPI in PRR is 0.

Each side has a shift register; the master supplies the clock on SCK. Data leaves the master on MOSI and returns on MISO. As master the SPI does not drive SS itself; software pulls the slave's SS low, then writing SPDR starts the clock and eight bits move; the clock then stops and SPIF is set, raising an interrupt if SPIE in SPCR is set. The master may write the next byte or end the packet by raising SS. As slave, while SS is high the SPI sleeps with MISO tri-stated and SPDR can be loaded, but nothing shifts until SS goes low; SPIF is set after each complete byte. The last received byte stays in the buffer. Transmit is single buffered, so SPDR cannot be written until the shift finishes; receive is double buffered, and a byte must be read before the next one completes or it is lost. As slave, SCK low and high periods must each be longer than 2 CPU clock cycles. With the SPI on, the directions of MOSI, MISO, SCK and SS are overridden (SPI pin overrides).

In slave mode SS is always an input: low activates the SPI and lets MISO drive if set as output, with every other pin an input; high makes every pin an input, stops reception and at once resets the send and receive logic, discarding a partly received byte, which keeps the slave's bit count aligned with the master. In master mode (MSTR set) SS may be an output, then an ordinary output pin with no effect on the SPI. If SS is an input it must be held high; pulled low, the SPI takes it as another master selecting it: MSTR is cleared, the SPI becomes a slave, MOSI and SCK become inputs, and SPIF is set (interrupting if enabled with the I-bit set). An interrupt-driven master that may see SS pulled low should check MSTR in its handler and set it again if it was cleared.

CPOL and CPHA give four combinations of clock polarity and phase. Data is shifted out on one SCK edge and sampled on the other, leaving time to settle. DORD = 0 sends the MSB first, DORD = 1 the LSB first.

A full-duplex USART with independent transmit and receive registers that works asynchronously or synchronously (clocked as master or as slave), and a high-resolution baud rate generator. Frames have 5 to 9 data bits and 1 or 2 stop bits, with hardware odd or even parity generation and checking. It detects data overrun and framing errors, filters noise (false start bit detection and a digital low-pass filter), and has three interrupts: receive complete, transmit complete and transmit data register empty. It also offers multi-processor communication and a double-speed asynchronous mode, and can work as an SPI master. The module runs only while PRUSART0 in PRR is 0.

Three parts share the control registers: the clock generator (baud rate generator plus synchronisation for an external clock in synchronous slave mode; pin XCKn serves synchronous mode only), the transmitter (one write buffer, a shift register, a parity generator and frame control, so frames can follow one another with no gap) and the receiver (clock and data recovery for asynchronous input, a parity checker, and a receive shift register feeding a two-level buffer, UDRn). It accepts every frame format the transmitter can send and flags frame errors, data overrun and parity errors.

Four clock modes: asynchronous at normal or double speed, and synchronous as master or as slave. UMSELn in UCSRnC chooses asynchronous or synchronous; U2Xn in UCSRnA sets double speed (asynchronous only). In synchronous mode (UMSELn = 1) the XCKn direction bit picks an internal clock (output, master) or an external one (input, slave).

Used for asynchronous and synchronous master modes. UBRRn feeds a down-counter clocked at fosc that reloads from UBRRn each time it reaches zero or when UBRRnL is written, producing one clock per pass: fosc/(UBRRn+1). The transmitter divides this by 2, 8 or 16 according to mode; the receiver's recovery units use it directly, with a state machine of 2, 8 or 16 states depending on UMSELn, U2Xn and DDR_XCKn. UBRRn spans 0 to 4095.

Setting U2Xn halves the baud divider from 16 to 8 and so doubles the asynchronous rate; it has no effect in synchronous mode, where it should be 0. The receiver then takes only 8 samples per bit instead of 16, so the baud setting and system clock must be more accurate; the transmitter loses nothing.

In synchronous slave mode XCKn is sampled by a synchronisation register against metastability and then passed through an edge detector, a delay of two CPU clocks that limits the XCKn frequency to below fOSC/4. fOSC depends on the stability of the clock source, so some margin is advised.

With UMSELn = 1, XCKn is the clock input (slave) or output (master). Input data on RxDn is sampled on the XCKn edge opposite to the one where output data on TxDn changes. UCPOLn = 0: data changes on the rising edge and is sampled on the falling edge; UCPOLn = 1: changes on falling, sampled on rising.

A frame is one start bit (always low), 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9 data bits sent least significant first, an optional even or odd parity bit after the data, and 1 or 2 stop bits (always high): 30 valid combinations. A frame may follow directly on the last one or the line may idle high. UCSZn2:0 sets the data bits, UPMn1:0 the parity and USBSn the stop bits, shared by receiver and transmitter; changing any of them corrupts transfers in progress in both directions. The receiver ignores the second stop bit, so a frame error is flagged only when the first stop bit is zero. Parity is the exclusive-or of the data bits, inverted for odd parity.

Set the baud rate, set the frame format, then enable the transmitter and/or receiver. For interrupt-driven use, keep global interrupts disabled while initialising. Before changing baud rate or frame format, make sure no transfer is under way: TXCn shows the transmitter has finished and RXCn that no unread data waits; if TXCn is used for this it must be cleared before each write to UDRn.

TXENn in UCSRnB enables the transmitter and takes over the TxDn pin; in synchronous mode the clock on XCKn drives the transfer. Writing UDRn loads the transmit buffer; the buffer moves to the shift register when that is idle, or right after the last stop bit of the frame in progress, and the frame goes out at the rate set by the baud register, U2Xn or XCKn. With frames under eight bits the top bits written to UDRn are ignored. For 9-bit characters (UCSZn = 7) the ninth bit goes into TXB8n in UCSRnB before the low byte is written to UDRn; it can mark address frames in multi-processor mode or carry protocol information.

UDREn is set while the transmit buffer is empty and can take new data, and cleared by writing UDRn; with UDRIEn set its interrupt runs for as long as UDREn is set, so the handler must write UDRn or disable the interrupt. TXCn is set once the whole frame has left the shift register and the buffer holds nothing new; it clears when its interrupt (TXCIEn) runs or when a one is written to it. TXCn suits half-duplex links such as RS-485, where the transmitter must release the bus as soon as it has finished. Write UDREn as zero when writing UCSRnA. With parity on (UPMn1 = 1) the parity bit is inserted after the last data bit. Clearing TXENn takes effect only after all pending data has been sent; the pin then returns to the port.

RXENn in UCSRnB enables the receiver and takes over the RxDn pin; in synchronous mode XCKn clocks the bits. Reception starts at a valid start bit; each bit is sampled and shifted in until the first stop bit, after which the frame moves into the receive buffer for reading from UDRn (a second stop bit is ignored). Bits above the frame size read as zero. For 9-bit characters read RXB8n in UCSRnB first, and the status flags FEn, DORn and UPEn in UCSRnA, before reading UDRn, because reading UDRn advances the buffer, where these bits are stored with the frame. RXCn is one while unread data is in the buffer; disabling the receiver empties the buffer and clears RXCn. With RXCIEn set the receive interrupt runs while RXCn is set, so the handler must read UDRn.

FEn, DORn and UPEn sit in the receive buffer with their frame, so read UCSRnA before UDRn. Software cannot set them, they raise no interrupt, and they should be written as zero whenever UCSRnA is written. FEn is one if the next frame waiting in the buffer had a zero first stop bit, useful for spotting lost sync, breaks and protocol handling; USBSn does not affect it. DORn means frames were lost: the buffer held two characters, another waited in the shift register and a new start bit arrived; it clears when a frame moves successfully into the buffer. UPEn is one when the next frame in the buffer failed the parity check, and always zero with parity checking off. The parity checker runs when UPMn1 is set, UPMn0 choosing odd or even, and its result stays valid until UDRn is read.

operation.topic: USART0 disabling the receiver and flushing
operation.text: Unlike the transmitter, the receiver stops at once when RXENn is cleared: a frame being received is lost, the pin returns to the port and the buffer is flushed, losing its contents. To empty the buffer during normal operation, for example after an error, read UDRn until RXCn clears.

The receiver samples RxDn at 16 times the baud rate (8 times in double speed). A high-to-low transition starts start-bit detection; counting the first low sample as 1, samples 8, 9 and 10 (normal) or 4, 5 and 6 (double speed) decide by majority whether the start bit is real; if two or more are high it is treated as a noise spike and the receiver waits for the next falling edge. A valid start bit synchronises the recovery logic, once per frame. Double speed gives a larger timing uncertainty.

Once synchronised, the data recovery state machine has 16 states per bit (8 in double speed). Each bit, the parity bit and the first stop bit are decided by majority of the three centre samples, which acts as a low-pass filter on RxDn. A stop bit read as 0 sets FEn. The next start bit may begin right after the last voting sample of the stop bit in normal mode, and slightly later in double speed; this early detection affects the receiver's operating range.

The receiver tolerates only a limited mismatch between the incoming bit rate and its own baud rate; beyond it, frames cannot be synchronised to the start bit. The recommended maximum receiver errors assume the total error is split equally between receiver and transmitter; normal speed tolerates more variation than double speed. The receiver's error has two sources: the system clock, which drifts somewhat with supply and temperature (seldom a problem with a crystal, but a resonator may be more than 2 % off), and the baud generator, which cannot always divide the clock exactly; choose a UBRRn value with a low enough error.

Setting MPCMn in UCSRnA makes the receiver drop frames that carry no address, so slaves sharing one bus with a master handle fewer frames; the transmitter is not affected. The frame type bit is the first stop bit for 5- to 8-bit frames, or the ninth bit (RXB8n) for 9-bit frames: one marks an address frame, zero a data frame. With 9-bit frames (UCSZn = 7) the master sets TXB8n for an address and clears it for data, and slaves also use 9-bit frames. Procedure: all slaves set MPCMn; the master sends an address frame, which every slave receives (RXCn set as usual); each slave reads UDRn, and the one addressed clears MPCMn while the rest keep it and wait for the next address; the addressed slave takes data frames until a new address frame arrives, the others ignore them; after its last data frame it sets MPCMn again. Using 5- to 8-bit frames works but is awkward, since the receiver must switch between n and n+1 bit formats, which hampers full duplex, and the transmitter must then use two stop bits. Do not set or clear MPCMn with SBI or CBI: it shares its I/O location with TXCn, which they can clear by accident.

The listed UBRRn settings give common asynchronous baud rates from standard crystal and resonator frequencies. Errors above 0.5 % are usable, but noise immunity falls as the error grows, especially with long frames.

Setting both UMSELn1:0 bits puts the USART in master SPI mode: full duplex over three wires, master only, all four SPI modes, MSB or LSB first, queued (double-buffered) operation, the high-resolution baud generator, up to fXCKmax = fCK/2, and flexible interrupts. The SPI logic then drives the USART's shift registers, buffers and baud generator directly; parity, clock and data recovery and the RX/TX control logic are switched off and replaced by one SPI transfer controller, while pin control and interrupt generation stay the same. The registers keep their addresses but some control bits change meaning.

Only the internal clock (master) is supported, so the XCKn direction bit must be set to output, preferably before TXENn and RXENn are set. The clock is the same as USART synchronous master mode, and so is the UBRRn equation.

UCPHAn and UCPOLn select one of four clock phase and polarity combinations; data shifts out on one XCKn edge and is sampled on the other. A frame is 8 data bits, MSB first or LSB first as UDORDn in UCSRnC selects, shared by receiver and transmitter; changing any of these settings corrupts transfers in progress. Frames may follow each other directly or the line may idle high. Writing two bytes to UDRn sends 16 bits, with the transmit complete interrupt marking the end.

Set the baud rate, make XCKn an output (which selects master), set the frame format and enable transmitter and receiver; only the transmitter can work alone. For interrupt-driven use keep global interrupts off during set-up. So that XCKn starts at once, UBRRn must be zero when the transmitter is enabled and receive its real value after that, before the first transfer; directly after reset UBRRn is already zero. Before re-initialising with a new baud rate, data mode or frame format, check with TXCn and RXCn that no transfer is in progress; if TXCn is used, clear it before each write to UDRn.

The transmitter must be enabled (TXENn), and takes over TxDn; enabling the receiver (RXENn) is optional and takes over RxDn; XCKn is the transfer clock either way. Every transfer, whether to send or to receive, starts with a write to UDRn, since the transmitter makes the clock. Read UDRn once for each byte sent to keep the input buffer in step. On overflow the most recent received byte is lost, not the oldest: send four bytes without reading and the third is the one lost. RXCn, TXCn and UDREn and their interrupts work as in USART mode; FE, DOR and PE are unused and read zero. Disabling transmitter or receiver works as in USART mode.

The master timing matches the SPI, and UCPOLn, UCPHAn and UDORDn match CPOL, CPHA and DORD. Differences: MSPIM is master only; its transmitter is double buffered where the SPI has no buffer; its receiver has one more buffer level; it has no write collision flag (WCOL) and no SPI2X, the same rate being reached through UBRRn; interrupt timing differs; pin control differs.

An I2C-compatible two-line interface for master and slave operation, as transmitter or receiver, with 7-bit addressing (up to 128 slave addresses), multi-master arbitration, data rates up to 400 kHz, slew-rate limited output drivers, spike suppression on the bus inputs, a fully programmable slave address with general call, and wake-up from sleep on address recognition. The bus is SCL (clock) and SDA (data), both bidirectional; each line needs only one pull-up resistor, and every device has its own address. The module runs only while PRTWI in PRR is 0.

Both lines are pulled up to the positive supply through resistors, and every compliant device drives them with open-drain or open-collector outputs, making a wired-AND: a line is low when any device pulls it low, and high only when all release it. Every AVR device on the bus must be powered for the bus to work. The number of devices is limited only by the 400 pF bus capacitance limit and the 7-bit address space. The TWI electrical characteristics give one set of limits for buses below 100 kHz and one for up to 400 kHz, including the pull-up resistor values.

Each data bit comes with a clock pulse, and SDA must be stable while SCL is high, except to signal START or STOP. The master starts a transfer with a START (SDA falling while SCL is high) and ends it with a STOP (SDA rising while SCL is high); in between the bus is busy. A START issued before a STOP is a REPEATED START, used to begin a new transfer without giving up the bus; the bus stays busy until the next STOP.

An address packet is 9 bits: 7 address bits sent MSB first, a READ/WRITE bit (1 = read) and an acknowledge bit. An addressed slave acknowledges by pulling SDA low in the ninth clock; a busy slave leaves SDA high, and the master can then send STOP or REPEATED START. SLA+R and SLA+W name address packets with read and write. Address 0000 000 is the general call, which all slaves set up for it acknowledge; it is meant for writing the same data to several slaves, and a general call with read makes no sense. Addresses 1111 xxx are reserved. A data packet is 9 bits too: one byte, MSB first, and an acknowledge from the receiver (low = ACK, high = NACK); after the last byte the receiver sends NACK. A transfer consists of START, an address packet, at least one data packet, then STOP; START followed directly by STOP is not allowed. A slave can hold SCL low to stretch the low period when it needs time, which slows the transfer without changing the high period the master sets.

operation.topic: TWI multi-master arbitration and clock synchronisation
operation.text: Several masters may start at once. The wired-AND SCL makes a combined clock whose high period is the shortest master high period and whose low period is the longest master low period; every master times its own high and low periods from the combined line. Each master watches SDA after driving it; a master that drives high but reads low has lost arbitration, must release SDA at once and switch to slave mode to see whether the winner addresses it, though it may keep clocking to the end of the current packet. Arbitration may run over many bits, into the data when masters address the same slave, and the slaves never notice. Arbitration must never be needed between a REPEATED START and a data bit, a STOP and a data bit, or a REPEATED START and a STOP; software must ensure this, so in a multi-master system every transfer must be built alike: an address packet followed by the same number of data packets.

operation.topic: TWI pins and bit rate generator
operation.text: The SCL and SDA output drivers have slew-rate limiting to meet the TWI specification, and the inputs suppress spikes shorter than 50 ns. Setting the PORT bits of the SCL and SDA pins turns on the internal pull-ups, which in some systems remove the need for external resistors. In master mode the bit rate generator sets the SCL period from TWBR and the prescaler bits in TWSR. Slave operation does not depend on these, but the slave's CPU clock must be at least 16 times SCL. Slaves stretching SCL low lower the average bus clock.

operation.topic: TWI bus interface, address match and control units
operation.text: The bus interface unit holds TWDR (the address or data byte to send or just received), a (N)ACK register that software cannot reach directly (set through TWCR when receiving, read through TWSR when transmitting), the START/STOP controller, which detects START and STOP even in sleep so an addressed MCU can wake, and arbitration detection, which tells the control unit when a master transfer loses arbitration. The address match unit compares received addresses with the 7-bit address in TWAR, and with the general call address when TWGCE is set, also in sleep; whether the TWI acknowledges depends on TWCR. The control unit sets TWINT when an event needs software and updates TWSR with a status code in the next clock; TWSR is valid only while TWINT is set and otherwise reads a no-information code. SCL is held low as long as TWINT is set. TWINT is set after a START or REPEATED START has been sent, after SLA+R/W or an address byte has been sent, after losing arbitration, after being addressed by its own address or a general call, after receiving a data byte, after a STOP or REPEATED START received while still addressed as slave, and on a bus error from an illegal START or STOP.

The TWI works byte by byte and raises an interrupt after every bus event, so software is free during each byte. TWIE in TWCR together with the I-bit in SREG decides whether TWINT raises an interrupt; otherwise software polls TWINT. With TWINT set, TWSR tells the bus state and software sets up TWDR and TWCR for the next bus cycle, then writes TWCR with TWINT set; writing a one to TWINT clears it, and the TWI does nothing while it is set, so clearing it starts the next operation. A master sending one byte to a slave: write TWCR to send START; when TWINT sets, check TWSR for START sent, load SLA+W into TWDR and write TWCR to send it; when TWINT sets, check TWSR for SLA+W sent and ACK received, load the data into TWDR and write TWCR to send it; when TWINT sets, check for data sent and ACK received, then write TWCR to send STOP. TWINT is not set after a STOP has been sent.

Two master modes, transmitter (MT) and receiver (MR), and two slave modes, transmitter (ST) and receiver (SR); one application may use several (for example MT to write a TWI EEPROM and MR to read it back, with SR when another master sends to it). Status codes are given with the prescaler bits of TWSR masked to zero; the TWI transfer waits while TWINT is set until software clears it. In transfer diagrams S is START, Rs REPEATED START, R a read bit (SDA high), W a write bit (SDA low), A an acknowledge (SDA low), A with overbar a not-acknowledge (SDA high), Data an 8-bit byte, P STOP and SLA the slave address.

A master mode starts with a START; the address packet then decides MT (SLA+W) or MR (SLA+R). TWEN enables the TWI, TWSTA asks for START and writing TWINT to one clears the flag; the TWI waits for a free bus and sends START, then sets TWINT with status 0x08. Load SLA+W into TWDR and clear TWINT to send it; afterwards the status is 0x18, 0x20 or 0x38. Then write each data byte to TWDR and clear TWINT. TWDR may be written only while TWINT is high; otherwise the write is discarded and TWWC is set. The transfer ends with STOP or a REPEATED START (status 0x10), which lets the master address the same or another slave, or switch between MT and MR, without releasing the bus.

A successful write runs 0x08 (START sent), 0x18 (SLA+W acknowledged), then 0x28 after each acknowledged byte, before STOP. A REPEATED START gives 0x10, from which SLA+W continues in MT or SLA+R moves to MR. NACK after the address gives 0x20 and NACK after a data byte 0x30. Losing arbitration in the address or a data byte gives 0x38; losing it and being addressed as a slave leads to the slave states 0x68, 0x78 or 0xB0.

Started like MT with a START (status 0x08), then SLA+R is loaded into TWDR and TWINT cleared; the status is then 0x38, 0x40 or 0x48. Each received byte can be read from TWDR while TWINT is set. After the last byte the master returns NACK to tell the slave transmitter to stop, then sends STOP or REPEATED START with the same TWCR values as in MT. A REPEATED START (0x10) lets it address the same or another slave, or switch to MT, keeping the bus. A successful read runs 0x08, 0x40, 0x50 for each acknowledged byte and 0x58 for the last, not acknowledged, byte; NACK after the address gives 0x48 and lost arbitration 0x38.

Load TWAR with the device's own 7-bit address in the upper bits, and its LSB (TWGCE) set to answer the general call, then write TWCR with TWEN = 1, TWEA = 1 (acknowledge own address or general call) and TWSTA = TWSTO = 0. The TWI then waits to be addressed; a direction bit of 0 (write) enters SR, 1 enters ST. After its address and the direction bit, TWINT sets and TWSR holds the status. SR can also be entered after losing arbitration as master (0x68, 0x78). Clearing TWEA during a transfer returns NACK after the next byte, signalling that no more can be taken; while TWEA is 0 the own address is not acknowledged, though the bus is still watched and setting TWEA resumes recognition, so TWEA can isolate the TWI from the bus for a while. In every sleep mode except Idle the TWI clock is off, yet with TWEA set it still answers its own address (or the general call) by running on the bus clock; the part then wakes and holds SCL low until TWINT is cleared, after which reception carries on normally. A long start-up time can hold SCL low for long and block other traffic. After waking this way TWDR does not hold the last byte on the bus.

Own address with write, acknowledged, gives 0x60, then 0x80 for each acknowledged byte and 0xA0 when STOP or REPEATED START arrives; a last byte answered with NACK gives 0x88. The general call path is 0x70, 0x90 per byte, 0x98 for a NACKed last byte, and 0xA0. After losing arbitration as master, being addressed gives 0x68 (own address) or 0x78 (general call).

Set up TWAR and TWCR as for SR; a direction bit of 1 (read) after the own address enters ST, which can also follow lost arbitration (0xB0). If TWEA is cleared during the transfer, the TWI sends the last byte, enters 0xC0 or 0xC8 depending on whether the master answers NACK or ACK, then switches to not-addressed slave mode and ignores the master if it continues, so the master reads all ones. 0xC8 means the master asked for more (ACK) after the intended last byte. TWEA = 0 stops recognition of the own address while the bus is still watched; setting it resumes. Sleep behaviour (wake on address with SCL held low until TWINT is cleared, TWDR not holding the last bus byte) is the same as in SR. A normal read runs 0xA8 (own SLA+R acknowledged), 0xB8 per acknowledged byte, and 0xC0 when the master NACKs.

Two codes match no defined state. 0xF8 means no information, as TWINT is clear; it is seen between states and when the TWI takes no part in a transfer. 0x00 is a bus error: a START or STOP at an illegal place in a frame, such as in the middle of a byte or of an ACK bit; TWINT is set. To recover, set TWSTO and clear TWINT by writing a one to it: the TWI enters not-addressed slave mode and clears TWSTO, leaving the other TWCR bits alone, and SDA and SCL are released without a STOP being sent.

Some jobs need more than one mode, such as reading a serial EEPROM: the master starts the transfer, writes the location to read in MT mode, reads the data in MR mode and ends the transfer. The direction change is made with a REPEATED START between sending the address byte and receiving the data, so the master keeps the bus throughout; in a multi-master system another master could otherwise move the EEPROM's data pointer between the two steps.

When several masters start at once the TWI protocol lets one of them finish with no data lost. Masters doing exactly the same transfer to the same slave never notice the contention, nor does the slave. Masters that address one slave but differ in data or in the direction bit lose arbitration in the READ/WRITE bit or the data bits, the one sending a one against a zero losing; losers go to not-addressed slave mode or wait for a free bus and send a new START, as software chooses. Masters addressing different slaves arbitrate in the address bits; a loser switches to slave mode and, if the winner addresses it, to SR or ST according to the READ/WRITE bit, otherwise to not-addressed slave mode or waiting for a free bus. Status codes after losing arbitration: 0x38 if not addressed (bus released, or a START sent when the bus is free), 0x68 or 0x78 if addressed for a write, 0xB0 if addressed for a read.

The comparator weighs the positive input AIN0 against the negative input AIN1 and sets its output ACO while AIN0 is the higher of the two. Its output can fire the Timer/Counter1 input capture, and it has an interrupt of its own that can be set to trigger on a rising edge, a falling edge or either edge of the output. Using the ADC multiplexer for its negative input needs PRADC in the power reduction register written to 0.

Any of the ADC7..0 pins can stand in for AIN1. This borrows the ADC multiplexer, so the ADC has to be off: with ACME (ADCSRB) set and ADEN (ADCSRA) clear, MUX2..0 in ADMUX pick the pin. With ACME clear or ADEN set, AIN1 is the negative input.

Setting ACD in ACSR removes power from the comparator, which lowers the current in Active and Idle modes; it can be set at any time, but ACIE should be cleared first or the change itself may raise an interrupt. Setting ACBG puts the fixed bandgap reference on the positive input in place of AIN0; the reference needs time to settle and a first result taken before then may be wrong. ACO is the synchronised comparator output and lags it by 1 to 2 clock cycles. ACI is set by the output event chosen with ACIS1:0; the interrupt runs when ACIE and the global I-bit are set, and ACI clears when the vector runs or when a one is written to it.

A 10-bit successive approximation converter behind an 8-channel analog multiplexer; every input is single ended and measured against 0 V (GND). A sample and hold keeps the input steady for the length of a conversion. The ADC has its own analog supply pin, AVCC, which must stay within ±0.3 V of VCC. On-chip references of nominally 1.1 V and AVCC are available and either can be switched onto AREF with the REFSn bits in ADMUX, where an external capacitor improves noise performance. PRADC in the power reduction register must be 0 for the ADC to work. Code 0 stands for GND and the top code for the AREF voltage less 1 LSB.

The MUX bits in ADMUX choose the input: any ADC pin, GND, or the fixed bandgap reference. ADEN in ADCSRA turns the ADC on, and reference and channel choices only take effect once it is set. With ADEN clear the ADC draws no power, so it should be switched off before the power-saving sleep modes. The 10-bit result sits in ADCH and ADCL, right adjusted unless ADLAR in ADMUX is set. With a left-adjusted result and 8 bits enough, reading ADCH alone will do; otherwise ADCL is read first and then ADCH.
