Reading ADCL locks both data registers against the ADC until ADCH is read, so a conversion that ends in between is discarded, though its interrupt still fires.

With PRADC at 0, writing a one to ADSC starts a single conversion; ADSC reads one until the conversion is done and hardware then clears it. A channel change made during a conversion waits until that conversion ends. Auto triggering (ADATE in ADCSRA) starts a conversion on each rising edge of the source picked by ADTS in ADCSRB, and the edge also resets the ADC prescaler, giving conversions at fixed intervals. A trigger still high when a conversion ends does not start another, and an edge arriving during a conversion is ignored. The source's interrupt flag is set even with its interrupt disabled or the global I-bit clear, so conversions can be triggered with no interrupt, but that flag has to be cleared before the next event can trigger again.

Choosing the ADC interrupt flag itself as the trigger makes the ADC start the next conversion as soon as one finishes, so the data register is refreshed continuously whether or not ADIF is cleared. The first conversion is started by writing ADSC to one. With auto triggering on, a write of one to ADSC still starts a single conversion, and ADSC reads one during any conversion however it was started.

For full 10-bit resolution the converter wants a clock of 50 kHz to 200 kHz; a faster clock gives a higher sample rate at lower resolution. A 7-bit prescaler divides the system clock by 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 or 128 (ADPS bits in ADCSRA), which suits any CPU clock above 100 kHz; it runs while ADEN is set and is held reset while ADEN is low. A conversion started with ADSC begins on the next rising edge of the ADC clock. A normal conversion takes 13 ADC clocks and samples 1.5 clocks after its start; the first conversion after ADEN is set takes 25 clocks, sampling at 13.5, while the analog circuitry starts up. At the end of a conversion the result is written, ADIF is set and, in single conversion mode, ADSC clears at the same moment, so software can start the next one at once. With auto triggering the prescaler is reset by the trigger, sampling falls two ADC clocks after the trigger's rising edge, and synchronisation adds three CPU clocks. In free running mode a new conversion starts as soon as one completes, with ADSC staying high. When the bandgap is the input it needs time to settle, and the first reading after the first conversion may be wrong.

The MUXn and REFS1:0 bits pass through a temporary register so the selection changes only at a safe point. The selection follows the register until a conversion starts, is frozen during the conversion so the input gets its full sampling time, and follows again from the last ADC clock before the conversion completes (when ADIF sets). Since a conversion begins on the ADC clock edge after ADSC is written, ADMUX should not be given new values until one ADC clock after that write. With ADATE and ADEN both set a trigger can come at any moment, and an ADMUX change then may or may not apply to the next conversion. ADMUX is safe to change while ADATE or ADEN is clear; during a conversion, at least one ADC clock after its trigger; or after a conversion, before the flag serving as trigger is cleared. A change made in one of these windows applies to the next conversion.

In single conversion mode the channel is chosen before the conversion is started; it may be changed one ADC clock after ADSC is written, though waiting for the conversion to finish is simplest. In free running mode the channel is chosen before the first conversion; after that, a change made once the first conversion ends shows up one result late, because the following conversion has already begun on the old channel.

VREF sets the span of the conversion, and an input above VREF gives codes near 0x3FF. VREF can be AVCC, the internal 1.1 V reference or the voltage on AREF. AVCC reaches the ADC through a passive switch, and the 1.1 V reference is the bandgap (VBG) buffered by an internal amplifier; either way AREF is wired straight to the ADC, so a capacitor from AREF to ground makes the reference quieter, and VREF can be measured at AREF with a high-impedance meter. VREF is a high-impedance source and should carry only a capacitive load. When a fixed voltage source drives AREF, the internal choices must not be used, as they would be shorted to it; with nothing driving AREF the application can switch between AVCC and 1.1 V. The first result after a reference change may be off and is best thrown away.

The ADC can convert while the CPU sleeps, in ADC Noise Reduction or Idle mode, which keeps noise from the core and I/O off the measurement. The ADC is enabled and idle, single conversion mode is selected and the conversion complete interrupt is enabled; entering the sleep mode then starts a conversion once the CPU has stopped. If no other interrupt comes first, the ADC interrupt wakes the CPU and its routine runs; if another interrupt wakes the CPU earlier, that one runs and the ADC interrupt follows when the conversion ends, the CPU staying awake until the next sleep instruction. Other sleep modes do not switch the ADC off, so ADEN should be cleared before them to save current.

Every ADCn pin carries its pin capacitance and input leakage whether or not it is the selected channel. A selected channel's source charges the sample-and-hold capacitor, 14 pF, through a series resistance of 1 kΩ to 100 kΩ in the input path; the capacitor's far side sits at VCC/2. Sources of about 10 kΩ or less suit the ADC and make the sampling time negligible; a higher source impedance needs longer to charge the capacitor, by an amount that varies widely, so low-impedance sources and slowly varying signals work best. Signal content above the Nyquist frequency, fADC/2, should be removed with a low-pass filter before the input to avoid distortion.

To keep EMI from the digital circuits out of critical measurements: keep analog tracks short, run them over the analog ground plane and away from fast digital tracks; supply AVCC from VCC through an LC network (10 µH series, 100 nF to ground); use the noise canceler; and do not let any ADC3..0 pin used as a digital output switch during a conversion. Two-wire interface activity on ADC4 and ADC5 disturbs only conversions on those two channels.

For an n-bit single-ended ADC the range from GND to VREF is cut into 2^n steps (LSBs), coded 0 to 2^n − 1. Offset is how far the first transition (0x000 to 0x001) sits from its ideal place at 0.5 LSB; ideally 0 LSB. Gain error, taken after offset is removed, is how far the last transition (0x3FE to 0x3FF) sits from its ideal place 1.5 LSB below full scale; ideally 0 LSB. Integral non-linearity (INL), after offset and gain are removed, is the largest distance of any transition from its ideal place; ideally 0 LSB. Differential non-linearity (DNL) is the largest departure of any code width from the ideal 1 LSB; ideally 0 LSB. Quantisation error is always ±0.5 LSB, since a 1 LSB wide band of inputs shares one code. Absolute accuracy is the largest distance of any unadjusted transition from its ideal place, combining offset, gain, differential and integral errors and quantisation; ideally ±0.5 LSB.

An on-chip temperature sensor is the single-ended channel ADC8, selected by writing 1000 to MUX3..0 in ADMUX, which also enables the sensor. The internal 1.1 V reference must be the ADC reference for this measurement, and the ADC is used in single conversion mode. The voltage rises linearly with temperature at roughly 1 mV/°C, and the temperature reads to within ±10 °C. The voltage differs between chips with process spread; for better accuracy, an offset found in production test can be stored per chip (in a register or EEPROM) and applied in software.

A change to REFS1:0 or MUX3:0 made while a conversion runs takes effect when that conversion completes (ADIF set). The internal reference choices may not be used while an external voltage is applied to AREF. A change to ADLAR alters the data register presentation at once, even during a conversion. Bit 4 of ADMUX is unused and reads zero.

debugWIRE is a single bidirectional wire through which a debugger steers program flow, runs AVR instructions on the CPU and programs the non-volatile memories. It is active when the DWEN fuse is programmed and the lock bits are unprogrammed: the RESET pin then becomes an open-drain (wired-AND) bidirectional line with its pull-up on, carrying dW between target and emulator, with the target powered from 1.8 V to 5.5 V. The system clock stays whatever the CKSEL fuses select. For the link to work, any pull-up on dW/RESET must be 10 kΩ or more (none is needed), RESET must not be tied straight to VCC, capacitors on RESET must be removed, and every external reset source must be disconnected.

Program memory break points use the AVR BREAK instruction: the debugger stores the instruction it replaces and runs it when execution resumes; a BREAK can also be written into the program by hand. Each change of break points reprograms the Flash, which shortens its data retention, so parts used for debugging should not go to end customers. Because dW shares the RESET pin, an external reset source cannot be used with debugWIRE enabled. A programmed DWEN fuse keeps parts of the clock system running in every sleep mode, raising sleep current, so DWEN should be unprogrammed when debugWIRE is not in use. The DWDR register passes data from the running program to the debugger and is reachable only through debugWIRE, not as a general purpose register.

The ATmega48A/48PA have neither read-while-write support nor a separate boot loader section, and SPM can run from anywhere in the Flash (when the SELFPRGEN fuse is programmed). Code can therefore load new program code over any interface and write it into its own Flash. The Flash is written a page at a time and a page must be erased before it is written. SPM loads a temporary page buffer word by word, either before erasing or between erasing and writing. To change only part of a page the rest must be saved first (for instance in the buffer) and written back; filling the buffer before the erase allows read-modify-write, while after the erase the old data can no longer be read. The buffer may be filled in any order, and the erase and write must address the same page.

The buffer clears itself after a page write, when RWWSRE in SPMCSR is written, and after a system reset. Each buffer address can be written only once until the buffer is cleared. An EEPROM write in the middle of page loading loses all the data loaded so far.

SPM takes its address from the Z-pointer (R31:R30). As the Flash is divided into pages, the program counter splits into low bits that select a word within a page (PCWORD) and high bits that select which page (PCPAGE). Page erase and page write are addressed separately, so software must give both the same page. LPM also uses Z and, reading the Flash byte by byte, uses Z0 as well. While an EEPROM write is under way, software cannot program the Flash or read the fuse and lock bits; checking that EEPE in EECR is clear before writing SPMCSR avoids this.

operation.topic: Reading fuse and lock bits from software
operation.text: Software can read the lock bits and every fuse byte. Z is loaded with the address of the byte wanted, BLBSET and SPMEN in SPMCSR are set, and an LPM within three CPU cycles returns the byte in its destination register. BLBSET and SPMEN clear themselves when the read is done, or when no LPM follows within three CPU cycles or no SPM within four; LPM then behaves normally. A programmed bit reads 0 and an unprogrammed bit reads 1.

Too low a supply can corrupt the Flash in two ways: a Flash write needs a minimum voltage to complete correctly, and the CPU can execute instructions wrongly below its operating voltage. Either of two measures prevents it. Hold the device in reset while the supply is too low, with the internal brown-out detector if its level matches the operating voltage or with an external low-VCC reset circuit; a write already in progress at reset still completes if the supply is high enough. Or keep the core in Power-down sleep while VCC is low, so no instruction can reach SPMCSR.
RWWSB always reads zero on the ATmega48A/48PA. Boot code that checks it anyway stays compatible with the devices that have read-while-write.

On the ATmega88A/88PA/168A/168PA/328/328P a boot loader held in Flash can receive program code over any interface and write it to the Flash, or read code back, while code keeps running (read-while-write). Code in the boot loader section can write the whole Flash, its own section included, so a boot loader can update or even erase itself. Its size is set by fuses, and two sets of boot lock bits, set independently, choose how each section is protected.

The Flash is split into an application section and a boot loader section (BLS), their sizes set by the BOOTSZ fuses, each with its own lock bits. Application code lives in the application section, protected by boot lock bits 0 (BLB0); SPM is disabled when executed from it, so it can never hold boot loader code. Boot loader code must sit in the BLS, the only place SPM can start programming from; from there SPM reaches the whole Flash. The BLS is protected by boot lock bits 1 (BLB1).

Separately from the BOOTSZ split, the Flash has two fixed sections: read-while-write (RWW) and no-read-while-write (NRWW). Erasing or writing a page in the RWW section leaves code in the NRWW section readable and the CPU running; erasing or writing a page in the NRWW section halts the CPU for the whole operation. The name describes the section being programmed, not the one being read. Code in the RWW section can never be read while a boot loader operation is in progress; a call, jump, LPM or interrupt into it can leave software in an unknown state, so interrupts are disabled or moved to the BLS, which always lies in the NRWW section. RWWSB in SPMCSR reads one while the RWW section is blocked, and software must clear it after programming (by writing RWWSRE) before running code there.

With no boot loader the whole Flash is free for application code. The boot lock bits can protect the whole Flash from software updates, only the BLS, only the application section, or neither. They can be set by software or by a serial or parallel programmer, and only a chip erase clears them. The general lock bits do not govern SPM and LPM: lock bit mode 2 does not stop SPM writing the Flash, and lock bit mode 1 does not stop LPM or SPM.

The application enters the boot loader by a jump or call, prompted for instance by a command arriving on the USART or SPI. Alternatively the BOOTRST fuse can point the reset vector at the start of the BLS, so the boot loader runs after every reset and can start the application once it is loaded. The MCU cannot change its own fuses: once BOOTRST is programmed, only a serial or parallel programmer can change it back.

operation.topic: Z-pointer addressing in the boot loader
operation.text: As on the ATmega48A/48PA, Z holds the SPM address, its low part selecting the word in a page and its high part which page, and erase and write must be given the same page. Once an operation starts its address is latched and Z is free for other use. Setting the boot loader lock bits is the one SPM operation that ignores Z. LPM uses Z0 as a byte select.

Page programming follows the ATmega48A/48PA procedure: erase a page before writing it, fill the temporary buffer word by word with SPM before the erase or between erase and write, keep any part of a page that must survive, and give erase and write the same page address. An erase or write in the RWW section leaves the NRWW section readable; in the NRWW section it halts the CPU.

With the SPM interrupt enabled, an interrupt is requested continuously while SPMEN in SPMCSR is clear, so it can replace polling SPMCSR. The interrupt vectors should then be moved to the BLS so no interrupt reaches the RWW section while it is blocked.

Leaving boot lock bit 11 unprogrammed lets the boot loader be rewritten, and an accidental write to it can destroy the boot loader and with it any further update. When the boot loader never needs to change, programming BLB11 shields it from software writes.

operation.topic: Keeping clear of the RWW section during self-programming
operation.text: The RWW section is unreadable throughout a page erase or page write, and software has to make sure nothing addresses it then; RWWSB stays set while it is busy. The interrupt vector table is moved to the BLS or interrupts are disabled for the duration. After programming, RWWSRE is written to clear RWWSB before the RWW section is used again.

operation.topic: Reading the signature row from software
operation.text: Z is loaded with the signature row address, SIGRD and SPMEN in SPMCSR are set, and an LPM within three CPU cycles returns that byte. SIGRD and SPMEN clear themselves after the read or when no LPM follows within three CPU cycles; LPM then works normally.

operation.topic: Preventing Flash corruption with a boot loader
operation.text: The measures for the ATmega48A/48PA apply (reset held during low supply, or Power-down sleep while VCC is low), and a third: when the boot loader never needs updating, programming the boot loader lock bits stops any software update of it. Any one measure is enough. Flash write times by SPM are the same, 3.7 ms to 4.5 ms per page erase, page write or lock bit write.

The ATmega48A/48PA have two lock bits and the ATmega88A/88PA/168A/168PA/328/328P six. Each is left unprogrammed (1) or programmed (0) to add protection, and only a chip erase returns them to 1. With no separate boot loader section, the ATmega48A/48PA allow SPM over the whole Flash when the SELFPRGEN fuse is programmed (0), and disable SPM otherwise.

There are three fuse bytes: extended, high and low. A programmed fuse reads as 0. Chip erase leaves the fuses unchanged, but programming LB1 locks them, so the fuses are programmed before the lock bits.

Fuse values are latched on entering programming mode, and a change takes effect only after the device leaves programming mode, except EESAVE, which takes effect immediately on programming. Power-up in normal mode latches the fuses too.

Every AVR carries a three-byte signature identifying the device, in its own address space, readable in serial and parallel mode even when the device is locked. A calibration value for the internal RC oscillator sits in the high byte of address 0x000 of the signature space and is copied into OSCCAL during reset so the oscillator runs at its calibrated frequency.

Parallel (high-voltage) programming writes and verifies the Flash, EEPROM, lock bits and fuses. Pulses are at least 250 ns long unless stated otherwise. In this mode port pins take programming signal names: PD1 is RDY/BSY (output), PD2 OE, PD3 WR, PD4 BS1, PD5 XA0, PD6 XA1, PD7 PAGEL, PC2 BS2, and PC[1:0]:PB[5:0] form the 8-bit bidirectional DATA bus. VCC and AVCC are both held at 4.5 V to 5.5 V (AVCC within 0.3 V of VCC), RESET takes +12 V, and XTAL1 is pulsed by the programmer. A positive XTAL1 pulse acts according to XA1/XA0; a WR or OE pulse acts according to the command loaded.

Start with the Prog_enable pins at 0000, RESET at 0 V and VCC at 0 V. Apply 4.5 V to 5.5 V between VCC and GND, making sure VCC passes 1.8 V within 20 µs. After 20 µs to 60 µs apply 11.5 V to 12.5 V to RESET, keep the Prog_enable levels steady for 10 µs or longer so the entry pattern is latched, and wait at least 300 µs before the first command. Where VCC cannot rise that fast: apply the supply, watch VCC and put 11.5 V to 12.5 V on RESET as soon as VCC reaches 0.9 V to 1.1 V, keep the Prog_enable pins steady for 10 µs or more, and wait for VCC to reach 4.5 V to 5.5 V before any command. Powering down or taking RESET to 0 V leaves programming mode.

The device keeps the loaded command and address. A command is loaded once for a run of reads or writes; 0xFF values need not be written after a chip erase (the whole Flash, and the EEPROM unless EESAVE is programmed); and the address high byte is loaded only when moving to a new 256-word Flash or 256-byte EEPROM window, which also holds for reading signature bytes.

Chip erase clears the Flash, the EEPROM (kept if EESAVE is programmed) and the lock bits; the lock bits are reset only after the program memory is fully erased, and the fuses are untouched. A chip erase is needed before the Flash or EEPROM is reprogrammed. To run it: XA1:XA0 = 10, BS1 = 0, DATA = 1000 0000, pulse XTAL1 to load the command, then pulse WR low; RDY/BSY goes low, and a new command waits until it returns high.

Flash data is gathered in a page buffer and a whole page is programmed at once. (A) Load the Write Flash command 0001 0000 (XA1:XA0 = 10, BS1 = 0, pulse XTAL1). (B) Load the address low byte (XA1:XA0 = 00, BS1 = 0). (C) Load the data low byte (XA1:XA0 = 01). (D) Load the data high byte (BS1 = 1, XA1:XA0 = 01). (E) With BS1 = 1, pulse PAGEL high to latch the word. (F) Repeat B to E until the buffer is full or all data for that page is loaded. The low address bits pick a word inside a page and the high bits pick which page; with fewer than 256 words per page, the top bits of the address low byte also help select a page during page write. (G) Load the address high byte (XA1:XA0 = 00, BS1 = 1). (H) Pulse WR low to program it, then wait until RDY/BSY returns high. (I) Repeat B to H for the rest of the Flash. (J) End by loading the No Operation command 0000 0000, which resets the internal write signals.

The EEPROM is also written a page at a time through a page buffer: load command 0001 0001, the address high byte, then for each byte the address low byte and the data, latching each with a PAGEL pulse; then with BS1 = 0 pulse WR low and let RDY/BSY return high before the next page. To read the Flash: load command 0000 0010 and the address high and low bytes, then with OE = 0 the low byte appears on DATA for BS1 = 0 and the high byte for BS1 = 1; set OE back to 1. To read the EEPROM: command 0000 0011, the address, then OE = 0 and BS1 = 0 put the byte on DATA.

operation.topic: Parallel fuse and lock bit programming
operation.text: Fuses are written with command 0100 0000 followed by a data low byte, in which a 0 programs a bit and a 1 erases it, then a WR pulse and a wait for RDY/BSY high. BS1 and BS2 choose the byte at the WR pulse: both 0 for the low byte, BS1 = 1 with BS2 = 0 for the high byte, BS1 = 0 with BS2 = 1 for the extended byte, returning BS1 or BS2 to 0 afterwards. Lock bits are written with command 0010 0000 and a data byte in which a 0 programs a bit; once LB mode 3 is programmed, no external programming mode can program the boot lock bits. Only a chip erase clears lock bits.

operation.topic: Parallel signature and calibration byte reading
operation.text: Signature bytes: load command 0000 1000 and an address low byte of 0x00 to 0x02, then OE = 0 and BS1 = 0 put the byte on DATA. The calibration byte: the same command with address 0x00, then OE = 0 and BS1 = 1. OE returns to 1 afterwards.

The Flash and EEPROM can be programmed over the SPI pins while RESET is held at GND: SCK and MOSI are inputs and MISO an output, mapped to PB5, PB3 and PB4. After RESET goes low the Programming Enable instruction must come before any program or erase instruction. The device runs from 1.8 V to 5.5 V during serial programming, with AVCC within 0.3 V of VCC and itself between 1.8 V and 5.5 V. A clock valid for the CKSEL fuses must be present; with the internal oscillator selected, XTAL1 needs no clock. In serial mode only, each EEPROM write erases the location first by itself, so no chip erase is needed; a chip erase sets every Flash and EEPROM location to 0xFF. SCK must stay low and high each for more than 2 CPU clock cycles when fck < 12 MHz, and more than 3 when fck ≥ 12 MHz.

Data into the device is clocked on rising SCK edges and data out on falling edges. Power up with RESET and SCK at 0; if the programmer cannot hold SCK low through power-up, pulse RESET high for at least two CPU clock cycles once SCK is 0. After at least 20 ms send Programming Enable on MOSI. When the link is in step, the second byte (0x53) comes back while the third byte is sent; all four bytes are sent either way, and if 0x53 does not return, RESET is pulsed and the instruction sent again. Flash is written a page at a time: each byte goes into a page buffer with Load Program Memory Page and the 6 LSB of the address, the low byte of a word before its high byte, and Write Program Memory Page with the 7 MSB of the address stores that page. Without RDY/BSY polling, wait at least tWD_FLASH before the next page; using the interface before a Flash write finishes can corrupt it. The EEPROM is written either a byte at a time with its write instruction (each location erased automatically first, waiting tWD_EEPROM without polling) or a page at a time with Load EEPROM Memory Page and Write EEPROM Memory Page, which change only the locations loaded. After a chip erase, 0xFF data need not be written. Any location can be read back on MISO. Setting RESET high ends the session and starts normal operation; to power off, set RESET high, then remove VCC.

The highest clock frequency depends on VCC: 4 MHz at 1.8 V, 10 MHz at 2.7 V and 20 MHz from 4.5 V to 5.5 V, rising linearly between 1.8 V and 2.7 V and between 2.7 V and 4.5 V. Operation below that limit is the safe operating area.

In master mode the numbered times run from SS low to the first SCK edge (6), the SCK period (1) and its high and low halves (2), the SCK rise and fall (3), MISO setup (4) and hold (5) about the sampling edge, and MOSI change after an SCK edge (7) and after the last edge (8). In slave mode they run from SS low to MISO valid (9), the SCK period (10), high and low times (11), rise and fall (12), MOSI setup (13) and hold (14), SCK edge to MISO change (15), last SCK edge to SS high (16), SS high to MISO tri-stated (17) and SS low to the first SCK edge (18).

On the bus, tLOW and tHIGH are the SCL low and high times and tof and tr the fall and rise times; tSU;STA and tHD;STA are the set-up and hold of a (repeated) START, tHD;DAT and tSU;DAT the data hold after and set-up before the SCL edges, tSU;STO the set-up of a STOP, and tBUF the free time between a STOP and the next START.

operation.topic: Typical characteristics: how they were measured
operation.text: The curves show typical behaviour and are not tested in production. Current was measured with every I/O pin an input with its internal pull-up on, clocked from a rail-to-rail square-wave generator. Active and Idle currents were taken with every bit of PRR set, so the I/O modules are off, and with the analog comparator disabled. Power-down current does not depend on the clock selected.

operation.topic: Typical characteristics: what sets the supply current
operation.text: Supply current depends on operating voltage, operating frequency, pin loading, pin switching rate, the code running and ambient temperature; voltage and frequency dominate. Parts are characterised above their tested frequency limits but are not ensured to work faster than their ordering code states. The watchdog timer's own current is the difference between Power-down current with the watchdog on and with it off.

operation.topic: ATmega48A: supply current of the I/O modules
operation.text: Each I/O module adds current in Active and Idle mode while its Power Reduction Register bit is clear. The absolute table gives the added current at three supply and clock points; the percentage table scales the current with every PRR bit set, so the total can be worked out for other VCC and frequency settings.

The AVR core executes arithmetic and logic, branch, bit and bit-test, data transfer and MCU control instructions. Most register operations take one clock; word add and subtract, the multiplies, data loads and stores and the jumps take two to four clocks; conditional branches take one or two clocks, and skips one to three. The direct JMP and CALL are present only on the ATmega168PA and ATmega328P.

The suffix of an ordering code gives package and temperature grade: AU 32A TQFP, MMH 28M1 VQFN, MU 32M1-A VQFN and PU 28P3 SPDIP for -40°C to 85°C; AN, MMN, MN and PN are the same packages for -40°C to 105°C, offered on the PA and P devices only (no 28M1 at 105°C for the ATmega168PA and ATmega328P). A trailing R means tape and reel. All devices run up to 20 MHz from 1.8 V to 5.5 V within the speed grade.
Silicon errata and data sheet clarifications for the ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/P are published separately as Microchip document DS80000855.
